summary:
## 1. EOD energetics / metabolic cost

The canonical direct measurement is **Salazar & Stoddard (2008, JEB 211:1012–1020)**, who pharmacologically partitioned the energy budget of *Brachyhypopomus pinnicaudatus* (now *B. gauderio*) into SMR, electrogenesis, and "other" (activity/muscle tone). **Males spend 11–22% of their total 24-h energy budget on EOD generation; females only 3%.** Split by phase: males 8.3% by day vs 12–26% at night; females 3.4% both. Standard metabolic rate: males 0.138 µl O₂ s⁻¹, females 0.0085 µl O₂ s⁻¹. Crucially, **cost scales superlinearly with amplitude**: O₂ per discharge vs. signal power fits *y* = 3.32×10⁻⁵·*x*^1.80 − 1.03×10⁻⁵ (R²=0.99) — i.e. an exponent of ~1.8 on power (mV² cm⁻¹). Circadian down-modulation is the cost-control knob: reducing discharge *rate* by day saves 70% (males)/62% (females); reducing waveform amplitude/duration saves 38–72% (males)/26% (females); combined 81–92% (males)/72% (females). **Stoddard & Salazar (2011, JEB 214:200–205)** put male *B. gauderio* at a **15% mean** of daily budget (females 3%), and contextualize this against acoustic signalers exceeding 50%.

**Salazar, Krahe & Lewis (2013, JEB 216:2459–2468)** is the definitive theory review. Key numbers: the *minimum* electrostatic dipole energy for an *Apteronotus leptorhynchus*-like field (~10 mV peak) is ~10⁻¹³ J ≈ 10⁶ ATP; for *Gymnotus carapo* (40 mV) ~10⁻¹¹ J ≈ 10⁸ ATP. **Dipole energy scales as Q², so doubling EOD amplitude quadruples the field energy** — the physical basis for a convex cost function. Cost is assumed proportional to EOD frequency (each cycle independent). Biological costs dwarf this floor: one pacemaker-neuron AP ≈ 10⁹ ATP; the whole PN (~120 P + 30 R neurons in *A. leptorhynchus*) ≈ 2×10¹¹ ATP per EOD cycle; one electrocyte AP ≈ 2×10¹⁰ ATP (Na⁺ currents in µA, ~20× the model P neuron's ~50 nA peak); ~1000 electrocytes in the *Eigenmannia* EO → ~2×10¹³ ATP/cycle = 8×10¹⁵ ATP s⁻¹ (1.7×10⁻⁶ J s⁻¹) at 400 Hz. Sensory side: ~15,000 P-units firing at ~1/3 EODf at 10⁷ ATP/spike → >10¹⁰ ATP per cycle; ~600 ELL spherical cells at EODf; ~5000 ELL pyramidal cells at 3–50 Hz. Synaptic processing could **double** all AP-based estimates. Whole-animal: routine *M*O₂ ≈ 7 µmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ for a 5 g male *Eigenmannia* (3×10¹⁶ ATP s⁻¹ = 2.5×10⁻³ J s⁻¹; 7×10¹³ ATP/cycle at 400 Hz) vs 3.7 µmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ for a 14 g *B. gauderio* (4×10¹⁶ ATP s⁻¹; 1.7×10¹⁵ ATP/pulse at 25 Hz). **Energy per unit time is nearly identical across wave/pulse types despite >10× difference per cycle — direct evidence for an amplitude↔frequency trade-off.** Summed EOD components ≈ **30% of routine consumption** for wave-type; but relative to scan-swimming (3–5× routine) the fraction falls to **5–10%**.

**Lewis, Gilmour, Moorhead, Perry & Markham (2014, J Neurosci 34:197–201)** measured AP cost at the organismal level in *Eigenmannia virescens* across 200–600 Hz and found **cost rises nonlinearly with rate**: Δ*M*O₂ [µmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ / Hz] = **0.003·exp(0.009·EODf)** — an exponential penalty for high-frequency signaling, arising from the cost of *maintaining AP amplitude* at high rates. Na⁺-influx-based estimates underestimate true cost when amplitude is held up. **Julian, Crampton, Wohlgemuth & Albert (2003, Oecologia 137:502–511)** — note the user's "Wykes" is actually **Wohlgemuth** — measured 34 individuals/23 species/all 5 gymnotiform families: mass-scaling exponent **0.74**, rates **~50% lower than temperate teleosts**; *M*O₂ was **independent of EOD type**, but scan swimming raised it **2.83±0.49-fold**. **Reardon et al. (2011, JEB 214:4141–4150)** found no normoxic correlation between metabolic rate and EODf or amplitude; under hypoxia EODf fell 3% but amplitude fell 31% (*Eigenmannia* 61% vs *Apteronotus* 29% under ASR90) — amplitude is the sacrificial variable. Regulatory mechanism: **Markham et al. (2009, PLoS Biol 7:e1000203)** — circadian/social Na⁺ channel trafficking in *Sternopygus macrurus* gives **39±5.5%** nightly amplitude increase costing **31% more ATP**; melanocortins can raise total EOD area by up to **340%**. **Markham & Stoddard (2005, J Neurosci 25:8746–8754)**: ACTH/α-MSH act via cAMP/PKA on electrocytes, enhancing amplitude and phase-2 duration within **6–45 min** (matching social-interaction timescales); 8-Br-cAMP mimics, PKI 14–22 blocks.

## 2. Predator-driven suppression / eavesdropping

**Stoddard (1999, Nature 400:254–256)**: a second EOD phase added to the ancestral monophasic pulse shifts spectral energy above the sensitivity band of electroreceptive predators; playbacks to *Electrophorus electricus* showed biphasic signals are less detectable. Freshwater ampullary predators detect DC and low-frequency (<~15 Hz, up to ~100 Hz) fields. **Stoddard, Tran & Krahe (2019, Front Ecol Evol 7:264)** is the best review: **any DC asymmetry creates low-frequency energy that stimulates predator ampullary receptors**; *B. gauderio* larvae start monophasic and over ~2 months develop a symmetric biphasic pulse suppressing the low-frequency spectrum. DC-balanced signals are unattractive to predators; DC-asymmetric ones highly attractive. In Panamanian *B. occidentalis*, high-predation streams (pimelodid *Rhamdia quelen*) show **peak-power frequency reduced by 130–320 Hz** vs low-predation streams (ANCOVA p<0.001); up to **45%** of fish carry damaged/regenerating tails in high-catfish streams. Males extend phase 2 to create DC asymmetry (attractive to females, conspicuous to predators) — the core honest-signal/predation trade-off. **Hanika & Kramer (1999, Naturwissenschaften 86:286–288)**: *Clarias gariepinus* detects male *Marcusenius macrolepidotus* EODs down to **103 µV_pp/cm** at up to **1.5 m**; males' EODs last ~**10×** longer than females'. **Hanika & Kramer (2000, Behav Ecol Sociobiol 48:218–228)**: threshold as low as **13 µV_pp/cm for 4-ms** monopolar square pulses. **Stoddard & Markham (2008, BioScience 58:415–425)** describe "signal cloaking": heterogeneous near-field components merge in the far field to cancel low-frequency spectrum, with males dynamically regulating cloaking. **Poon & Crampton (2026, Curr Biol 36:1621–1632.e7)** is new and directly relevant: 107,000 min of recordings over 27 nights from 6 loggers along 150 m of Amazon stream showed **bidirectional signal suppression** — *Electrophorus varii* pause low-voltage EODs before high-voltage strikes, and pulse-type knifefish **switch off their EODs for several seconds** on detecting eel signals. **Saenz et al. (2021, JEB 224:jeb242400)** document derived *loss* of complexity/plasticity in monophasic *B. bennetti*.

## 3–4. Rate modulation as social signal; social foraging

Mormyrid EOD *cessation* is a genuine submissive/hiding signal: **Kramer & Bauer (1976, Behav Ecol Sociobiol 1:45–61)** report chase-associated alternation of long bursts with **300–1000 ms discharge breaks**; aggressive discharge rate ≈ **2× isolated swimming, 3× resting**. **Terleph & Moller (2003, JEB 206:2355–2362)**: dominants increase EOD duration and shift relative phase amplitudes; physical contact unnecessary. Electrically silenced (nerve-cut) residents attacked less and elicited more attacks. Echo response: **Schuster (2001, JEB 204:1401–1412)** — fixed short-latency reply preventing EOD collision; novelty responses are evoked by amplitude changes as small as **1%** and latency changes of **0.1 ms**, effective only at baseline delays <**12.4 ms**. Chirps/JAR: **Field et al. (2019, Front Integr Neurosci 13:55)** show gymnotiform chirps double as JAR, with a ±60° (120°, = 6.7 ms at 50 Hz) critical interference window; *Brachyhypopomus* chirps average 21.14 s with 82.3% IPI decrease and 27.5% amplitude reduction. **Pedraja & Sawtell (2024, Nature 628:139–144)** is the flagship eavesdropping/collective-sensing result: *Gnathonemus petersii* uses conspecific EODs to extend detection range **up to 3-fold**, with ELL neurons resolving self- vs conspecific pulses at ~**12 ms** separation and a **5% LFP modulation** detection threshold.

## 5. Honest signaling

Classic chain: Zahavi (1975, 1977) → Grafen (1990) → Számadó (2011) → Penn & Számadó (2020, Biol Rev 95:267–290), who argue Grafen's model actually supports condition-dependent *differential costs*, not wasteful handicaps, and that Maynard Smith & Harper's (2003) **index** (unfakeable, physically constrained) should be separated from **handicap** (honest *because* costly). Applied to electric fish: **Gavassa et al. (2013, JEB 216:2403–2411)** — **body length explains up to 96% of EOD amplitude variance**, making amplitude near-index-like; male EOD ≈ **22%** of daily budget vs 3% female (**10× more**). **Gavassa et al. (2012, Anim Behav 83:935–944), "Signal modulation as a mechanism for handicap disposal"**, is the key conceptual paper: reliability *improved* under high competition (R²=0.95 field, R²=0.98 lab, density 2→12 fish/pool); because amplitude scales exponentially with length, cheating requires exponential cost. Modulation's main benefit is *shedding* the handicap when competition is low. Dawkins & Krebs (1978) / Krebs & Dawkins (1984) supply the manipulation-vs-information framing.

gaps_or_risks: Author-name correction: the oxygen-consumption paper is Julian, Crampton, WOHLGEMUTH & Albert (2003), not 'Wykes'. Cite as Wohlgemuth.

Species-name drift: Brachyhypopomus pinnicaudatus was reclassified as B. gauderio in 2008. Salazar & Stoddard (2008) uses pinnicaudatus; Stoddard & Salazar (2011), Gavassa et al. (2012, 2013) use gauderio. They are the same study system - do not treat as two species.

The widely quoted '30% wave / 20% pulse' figures are NOT direct measurements. The 30% is a theoretical bottom-up ATP summation for wave-type fish relative to ROUTINE MO2 (Salazar, Krahe & Lewis 2013); the same paper notes it drops to 5-10% relative to scan-swimming metabolism. Only the 11-22% (male) / 3% (female) pulse-type figures are experimentally partitioned. State the denominator explicitly or a reviewer will object.

Reardon et al. (2011) found NO relationship between metabolic rate and EOD frequency or amplitude under normoxia in wave-type fish - this directly tension-tests the 'EOD is expensive' narrative. Any modeling claim that EOD cost drives behavior should acknowledge this negative result.

Julian et al. (2003) similarly found MO2 independent of EOD type, attributing variance to scan swimming instead. The cleanest defensible claim is that cost scales with amplitude (superlinearly, exponent ~1.8-2.0) and with rate (exponentially per Lewis et al. 2014), not that total EOD cost is uniformly large.

Several key numbers were extracted via WebFetch summaries of paywalled pages (Gavassa et al. 2012 R^2 values; Markham et al. 2009 percentages; Field et al. 2019 chirp statistics) rather than from the primary PDFs. Verify these against the source PDFs before they go into a paper.

Could not retrieve full text for: Stoddard 1999 (Nature, 403), Stoddard & Markham 2008 (BioScience, paywalled - only abstract), Hanika & Kramer 2000 (403 on both Springer and the mirror), Lewis et al. 2014 full text (403; abstract + one equation obtained via PubMed/journal landing page). The Hanika & Kramer 13 uV_pp/cm threshold and the 103 uV_pp/cm / 1.5 m figures came from search-result summaries, not the papers themselves - verify.

The 45% tail-injury figure for B. occidentalis in high-predation streams came from a ScienceDirect topic-page summary, and the Frontiers 2019 review text I fetched did NOT confirm a specific percentage ('no specific percentages provided in text'). Trace this to its primary source (likely Hagedorn 1988, Copeia 1988:324-335, on Hypopomus occidentalis in Panama) before citing a number.

Poon & Crampton (2026, Curr Biol) is very recent; volume/page details (36(7), 1621-1632.e7) and DOI came from search results, not the article page (403). There is also an accompanying dispatch: Current Biology, S0960-9822(26)00301-5. Verify both.

Zahavi 1977 volume/pages (J Theor Biol 67(3):603-605) and its DOI were supplied from background knowledge, not verified in this session. Same for Maynard Smith & Harper 2003 ISBN, Gavassa et al. 2011 Horm Behav page range, Silva et al. 2007, Franchina & Stoddard 1998 DOI, and Moortgat et al. 2000 DOI. Check these against Crossref before compiling the bibtex.

Topic 3 request for mormyrid EOD cessation during submission is supported but thinly quantified in accessible sources: the 300-1000 ms discharge-break figure and the 2x/3x rate ratios trace to Kramer & Bauer (1976), whose full text I could not open (Springer 403). The 'long cessations as submissive appeasement' claim came from a search summary of a more recent paper. Get Carlson (2002, J Physiol Paris 96:403-417, 'Electric signaling behavior and the mechanisms of electric organ discharge production in mormyrid fish') for a citable review of cessation/pause semantics.

Topic 3 'sneaking'/signal cheating in electric fish is weakly covered in the literature. The closest defensible framing is Gavassa et al. (2012, 2013): cheating is constrained because EOD amplitude scales exponentially with body length. I found no paper documenting actual sneaker-male electric tactics in gymnotiforms - do not assert one exists.

arXiv:2511.08436 title differs between sources: the arXiv landing page gave 'Active Electrosensing and Communication in MARL-trained Weakly Electric Fish Collectives' while search results and the PDF URL show 'Understanding Electro-communication and Electro-sensing in Weakly Electric Fish using Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning' (likely a v1-to-v2 retitle). Check the current version before citing; this is the most direct prior work to the user's paper and also appeared at NeurIPS 2025.

Pedraja & Sawtell exists as both a 2023 bioRxiv preprint and the 2024 Nature paper; the quantitative details I extracted (3-fold range extension, 12 ms, 5% LFP threshold) came from the PREPRINT (PMC10515903). Numbers may have changed in the published version - verify against Nature 628:139-144.

The Frontiers in Zoology 2008 paper on Marcusenius pongolensis EOD plasticity (attractiveness vs predator-avoidance tradeoff, DOI 10.1186/1742-9994-5-7) could not be fetched (Springer 403) and its authorship was not confirmed. It is likely Hanika & Kramer but do not cite without checking.
